records.our_prose: Parsnips are light feeders and especially sensitive to excess nitrogen, which drives leafy tops and forked, hairy roots at the expense of a clean taproot. Clemson recommends a 5-10-10 fertilizer worked in before planting at about 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet, with an optional side-dressing of a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate when plants are about 4 inches tall. (Clemson HGIC) Avoid fresh manure entirely, and lean on well-finished compost rather than concentrated nitrogen.

records.our_prose: Parsnips want steady phosphorus and potassium for root development and only modest nitrogen, so a low-first-number blend such as 5-10-10 worked into the bed before sowing suits them well. Clemson gives a rate near 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet. Excess nitrogen is the classic parsnip mistake, producing lush tops and forked, hairy roots.

records.our_prose: Soil pH measures how acidic or alkaline your soil is, on a scale from 1 to 14 where 7 is neutral. Parsnips do best from about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. Very acidic soil, below about 5.5, holds them back and worsens problems like canker, so a soil test from your local extension office tells you your number and whether to add lime. Clemson suggests liming to about 6.0 to 6.5 for this group of root crops.
source_names: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
records.source_context: Fertilizing: It is best to base fertilizer and lime applications on the results of a soil test. The garden should be limed to a soil pH of 6.0 to 6.5 for the best growth of these root crops. If a soil test has not been taken, apply 5-10-10 fertilizer at 30 pounds per 1,000 square feet of garden before planting.

records.our_prose: Parsnip is a cool-season root that germinates and grows best at roughly 50 to 70°F and develops its sweet flavor only after near-freezing weather, so in peninsular Florida the late-spring and summer months (Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep) are far too hot to sow or grow it. The crop is handled as a fall-sown, winter-harvested vegetable, and those hot months carry no sowing or active growth. (Clemson HGIC)

records.our_prose: Parsnip's signature storage is in-ground overwintering. The roots are extremely frost-hardy and the cold converts starch to sugar, so in cold climates they are left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and dug as needed through winter and into early spring; UMN notes the later they are dug, the sweeter they are. (UMN Extension) For fall-dug roots, a root cellar or unheated garage near 32 to 40°F at high humidity is best, packing unwashed roots in damp sand, where they hold for months. (UMN Extension; Clemson HGIC) One caution: overwintered roots must be dug before they regrow in spring, since once the plant bolts in its second year the root turns woody.

records.our_prose: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most during the long, slow germination window and again as the roots size up. From sowing until the seedlings are up, often 2 to 3 weeks, the surface must stay moist and uncrusted. Once established, parsnips want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain.
records.source_context: If the soil becomes too dry, their growth may be seriously limited. Most vegetable crops require 1 inch of water per week for optimum pro- duction. If your area does not receive this amount of rainfall each week during the growing season, you will need to irrigate your garden using overhead sprinklers, soaker hoses, drip tape or hand watering.
